# Workflows in Agentic AI — Claude code workflows

[![DhanushKumar](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*-e2O4fDCA-W4cqGQ1IpOaQ.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@danushidk507?source=post_page---byline--8cac80792dd8---------------------------------------)

In an AI agent, a workflow is not just a prompt; it is a repeatable execution pattern where the **model gathers context, takes an action through tools, verifies the result, and then loops until the job is done**. Claude Code’s own docs describe this as an “ **agentic loop**” with three blended phases: **gather context, take action, and verify results.** They also show that the loop adapts to the task: a simple codebase question may only need context **gathering, while a bug fix or refactor can cycle through the loop many times.**

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*EvIeZ45h3wCxMi6zpXDJVw.png)

Anthropic’s Claude Code “ **Common workflows**” page is basically a cookbook for that loop. It covers understanding **new codebases, finding relevant code, fixing bugs, refactoring, working with tests, creating pull requests, handling documentation, working in notes and non-code folders, images, file and directory references, scheduled runs, session resume, parallel worktrees, plan-before-editing, delegating research to subagents, and piping Claude into scripts**. In other words, it is a set of production-oriented patterns for turning a language model into a **developer workflow engine rather than a one-shot chat assistant.**

### How Claude Code implements that workflow

Claude Code is an agentic assistant that runs in the terminal, and Anthropic says the same core loop also works in VS Code, JetBrains, the desktop app, Claude Code on the web, Slack, and CI/CD pipelines. The model does not just answer in text; it uses tools to read files, edit files, run commands, search the web, inspect code intelligence, and interact with other systems. Anthropic describe those built-in capabilities as the foundation of the agent, with extensions like s **kills, MCP, hooks, and subagents layered on top.**

The important design point is that Claude Code has direct access to your project files, terminal, git state, and project instructions in `CLAUDE.md`, plus auto memory and configured extensions. That is why it can do **multi-file tasks** such a **s “fix the authentication bug,” search for relevant files, read multiple components, make coordinated edits, run tests, and commit if asked**. This is also why it behaves differently from a narrow inline autocomplete tool: it is working with the whole project context, not just the current buffer.

The implementation details matter for agent design. Claude Code stores sessions locally as **JSONL under**`~/.claude/projects/`, supports **resume and forked sessions**, and **manages context by compacting older content when needed.** The docs also show that subagents get their own separate context window, which keeps the main conversation cleaner, and that planning can happen in a read-only mode before any edits touch disk.

### Why the recent Claude launch matters for workflows

The recent Claude 4 launch was explicitly about agentic work. Anthropic described Claude Opus 4 as its strongest coding model for long-running tasks and agent workflows, and Claude Sonnet 4 as a faster, more practical model with stronger instruction following. In the same announcement, Anthropic said Claude Code was generally available and had background tasks via GitHub Actions plus native integrations with VS Code and JetBrains. That is the product-level signal that Claude workflows are meant for real operational use, not just demos.

Anthropic also announced extended thinking with **tool use, parallel tool execution, and API capabilities like code execution, MCP connector support, Files API, and prompt caching**. The broader direction is clear: the **model reasons, calls tools, receives results, and continues the loop** with much better support for autonomous work. That is exactly the architecture you want for agent workflows that need to inspect code, fetch data, test, revise, and verify.

### How to think about the execution model

A useful mental model is to split the workflow into an **orchestrator and workers.** The orchestrator is **Claude**. The workers are your **tools: repository search, file reads, edits, test execution, web lookup, issue creation, or internal APIs.** With the Claude Messages API, Claude chooses whether to call a tool, emits a structured `tool_use` block, and your code executes the tool and returns a `tool_result` block. Anthropic’s docs show that with the default `tool_choice: auto`, Claude decides each turn whether to call a tool or answer directly, and that client-side tools run in your application while server tools run on Anthropic’s infrastructure.

There are two clean ways to build this. The first is the Client SDK approach, where you implement the tool loop yourself. The second is the Agent SDK, where Anthropic says the same tools, loop, and context management that power Claude Code are exposed as a library, and the SDK can handle tool execution for you. For production systems, many teams prototype with the SDK locally and then move to managed or hosted patterns later; Anthropic explicitly positions the Agent SDK as a library that runs the loop inside your own process, while Managed Agents move the runtime to Anthropic infrastructure.

### Prompt Recipes: The Foundation of Agentic Workflows

Most developers initially think prompting is simply asking a model to write code. Claude Code uses prompts differently. A prompt becomes a workflow trigger.

Anthropic’s workflow recipes are structured around a repeated pattern:

1. Explore
2. Understand
3. Plan
4. Execute
5. Verify
6. Commit

Instead of saying:

```
Fix this bug
```

the workflow prompt becomes:

```
Investigate the authentication failure.

First:
- locate all authentication flows
- identify possible root causes
- explain findings

Then:
- propose a fix

Do not edit anything until I approve the plan.
```

This seems simple but architecturally it changes everything.

The model is forced into a multi-stage execution cycle rather than immediate code generation.

Claude internally performs:

```
User Request
      │
      ▼
Repository Search
      │
      ▼
Context Collection
      │
      ▼
Reasoning
      │
      ▼
Plan Generation
      │
      ▼
Human Approval
      │
      ▼
Code Changes
      │
      ▼
Validation
```

This is why Claude Code often produces better engineering outcomes than raw API prompting. The workflow imposes structure before execution.

### Understanding New Codebases Workflow

One of the most powerful workflows documented by Anthropic is repository exploration.

Suppose a new engineer joins a project with:

```
500,000 lines of code
150 microservices
20 repositories
```

Traditional onboarding:

```
Read docs
Read code
Ask teammates
```

Claude workflow:

```
Analyze this repository.

Explain:
- architecture
- entry points
- authentication flow
- API layer
- database layer
- deployment process

Generate a system map.
```

Claude begins gathering context.

Internally the workflow becomes:

```
Find package.json
Find Dockerfiles
Find CI pipelines
Find API routers
Find DB configs
Find infrastructure files
```

Then it synthesizes:

```
System Architecture Report
```

This is effectively repository intelligence generation.

Anthropic explicitly recommends these exploration prompts because agent performance increases dramatically when the model first develops a mental map of the system.

### Resume Previous Conversations

This feature is extremely underrated.

Large engineering work rarely completes in one session.

Example:

Day 1

```
Analyze migration from Flask to FastAPI
```

Claude spends:

```
2 hours
500K tokens
```

collecting context.

Next day:

```
claude --resume
```

or

```
claude --continue
```

Claude restores:

```
Conversation history
Tool outputs
File discoveries
Previous reasoning
Execution state
```

instead of starting from scratch.

Internally:

```
Session Store
    │
    ▼
JSONL History
    │
    ▼
Tool Results
    │
    ▼
Context Recovery
```

This enables long-running engineering initiatives.

Example:

```
Week 1:
Architecture review

Week 2:
Migration planning

Week 3:
Implementation

Week 4:
Testing
```

all within the same cognitive thread.

Without session resumption the model repeatedly loses project memory.

With session resumption Claude behaves much closer to a persistent engineering collaborator.

### Parallel Sessions with Git Worktrees

This is where Claude becomes genuinely agentic.

Problem:

Three AI agents modify:

```
auth.py
auth.py
auth.py
```

simultaneously.

Result:

```
Merge conflict hell
```

Git worktrees solve this.

A worktree is an isolated checkout of the same repository.

Example:

```
git worktree add ../auth-worktree feature/auth
git worktree add ../ui-worktree feature/ui
git worktree add ../test-worktree feature/tests
```

Now:

```
Agent A
    └── auth-worktree

Agent B
    └── ui-worktree

Agent C
    └── test-worktree
```

Each agent gets:

```
Own filesystem
Own branch
Own changes
```

No collisions occur.

Architecture:

```
                 Main Repo
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼             ▼             ▼

Worktree A    Worktree B    Worktree C

Auth Agent    UI Agent      Test Agent
```

Anthropic specifically recommends worktrees for concurrent sessions because agent productivity drops dramatically when multiple workers edit the same checkout.

### Real Enterprise Example Using Worktrees

Imagine:

```
Payment Platform Migration
```

Tasks:

```
Frontend Updates
Backend Updates
Database Migration
Testing
Documentation
```

Instead of one agent:

```
Claude
 └── everything
```

Create:

```
Claude-Frontend
Claude-Backend
Claude-DB
Claude-Test
Claude-Docs
```

Each receives:

```
git worktree add
```

Each works independently.

Later:

```
git merge
```

or

```
open pull requests
```

This resembles a real software organization.

### Plan Before Editing

One of Claude Code’s most valuable capabilities is plan mode.

Plan mode is effectively:

```
READ ONLY AGENT
```

The model may:

```
Read files
Search repository
Analyze architecture
Build execution plan
```

but cannot write.

Workflow:

```
User Request
     │
     ▼

     │
     ▼
Implementation Plan

Provide:

- risks

```

```

```

This mirrors real software engineering processes.

Production teams almost never want autonomous edits before understanding impact.

### Delegate Research to Subagents

This is arguably the most advanced workflow currently available.

Anthropic’s subagents are independent Claude instances with:

```
Own context window
Own prompt
Own tools
Own permissions
```

They operate separately from the main agent.

Without subagents:

```
Main Agent
    ├── searches
    ├── logs
    ├── docs
    ├── stack traces
    ├── configs
    └── analysis
```

Context becomes polluted.With subagents:

```
Main Agent
     │
     ├── Research Agent
     ├── Test Agent
     ├── Security Agent
     └── Documentation Agent
```

Each performs independent work.

Returns:

```
Summary only
```

instead of entire search history.

Anthropic specifically designed subagents to prevent context flooding.

### A real scenario: fixing a failing authentication test in a codebase

A realistic workflow is this: CI fails on authentication tests, and your agent must inspect the failure, locate the relevant source files, patch the bug, and rerun the test suite. That maps directly to Claude Code’s documented pattern for fixing bugs efficiently: share the error, ask for fix recommendations, apply the fix, then verify with tests. It is also a good example of why subagents matter, because the search-and-read phase can be offloaded so the main context stays focused on the actual edit plan.

In a production setup, the workflow would usually look like this in execution order: the model sees the failing test output, decides to inspect the codebase, asks your tools to search for authentication-related files, reads the likely modules, proposes a minimal fix, writes the patch, runs tests again, and only then returns a final summary. Claude Code’s docs explicitly describe that pattern as the agentic loop, and Anthropic’s tool-use docs show the exact `tool_use` to `tool_result` exchange that makes it work.

### Production-ready example implementation

The example below uses the official Anthropic Python client and implements the tool loop explicitly so you can see how the workflow behaves end to end. It defines a small set of local tools for a codebase: search, read file, write file, and run a limited shell command. The model can repeatedly call those tools until it has enough evidence to fix the issue and verify it. This follows Anthropic’s documented pattern for client tools: you send `tools`, Claude returns `tool_use` blocks, your application executes them, and you send back `tool_result` blocks.

        "description": (\
            "Run a restricted command for verification only, such as tests, lint, or git diff. "\
            "The command is executed without shell=True and must use an allowlisted first token. "\
            "Use this to validate a fix, inspect test output, or check the working tree."\
        ),\
        "input_schema": {\
            "type": "object",\
            "properties": {\
                "command": {"type": "string", "description": "Command line to run, without shell operators."},\
                "cwd": {"type": "string", "description": "Optional working directory relative to the repo root."},\
                "timeout_sec": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 600, "default": 120},\
            },\
            "required": ["command"],\
            "additionalProperties": False,\
        },\
        "strict": True,\
    },\
]

def emit_event(event: str, **fields: Any) -> None:
    """
    Emit a single JSON log line for observability.

    Args:
        event: Stable event name.
        **fields: Additional structured fields.
    """
    record = {
        "ts": time.time(),
        "event": event,
        **fields,
    }
    print(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False), flush=True)

def ensure_within_repo(path: Path) -> Path:
    """
    Resolve a path and ensure it stays inside the repository root.

    Args:
        path: Candidate path.

    Returns:
        The resolved absolute path.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the resolved path escapes the repository root.
    """
    resolved = path.resolve()
    if resolved == REPO_ROOT or REPO_ROOT in resolved.parents:
        return resolved
    raise ValueError(f"Path escapes repository root: {path}")

def is_text_file(path: Path) -> bool:
    """
    Return True when the path is likely a text file that is safe to search.

    Args:
        path: File path.

    Returns:
        True for likely text files.
    """
    return path.suffix.lower() in READABLE_EXTENSIONS

def search_repo(query: str, max_results: int = 10) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Search repository files for a regex or plain text match.

    Args:
        query: Search pattern.
        max_results: Maximum number of returned hits.

    Returns:
        A JSON-serializable result payload.
    """
    try:
        pattern = re.compile(query)
    except re.error:
        pattern = re.compile(re.escape(query))

    hits: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
    for path in REPO_ROOT.rglob("*"):
        if len(hits) >= max_results:
            break
        if not path.is_file() or not is_text_file(path):
            continue
        try:
            if path.stat().st_size > MAX_FILE_BYTES:
                continue
            text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")
        except OSError:
            continue

        for idx, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), start=1):
            if pattern.search(line):
                hits.append(
                    {
                        "path": str(path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)),
                        "line": idx,
                        "snippet": line[:300],
                    }
                )
                if len(hits) >= max_results:
                    break

    return {"matches": hits, "count": len(hits)}

def read_file(path: str, start_line: int = 1, end_line: int | None = None) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Read a file from the repository with optional line boundaries.

    Args:
        path: Relative path under the repository root.
        start_line: One-based start line.
        end_line: Optional inclusive end line.

    Returns:
        File metadata and selected content.
    """
    file_path = ensure_within_repo(REPO_ROOT / path)
    if not file_path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"File not found: {path}")

    raw = file_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore")
    lines = raw.splitlines()
    start_idx = max(start_line, 1) - 1
    stop_idx = len(lines) if end_line is None else min(end_line, len(lines))
    selected = lines[start_idx:stop_idx]

    return {
        "path": str(file_path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)),
        "start_line": start_line,
        "end_line": stop_idx,
        "content": "\n".join(selected),
        "total_lines": len(lines),
    }

def write_file(path: str, content: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Write a file inside the repository root.

    Args:
        path: Relative path under the repository root.
        content: Full file contents.

    Returns:
        Confirmation metadata.
    """
    file_path = ensure_within_repo(REPO_ROOT / path)
    file_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp_path = file_path.with_suffix(file_path.suffix + ".tmp")

    tmp_path.write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")
    tmp_path.replace(file_path)

    return {
        "path": str(file_path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)),
        "bytes_written": len(content.encode("utf-8")),
        "status": "written",
    }

def is_allowed_command(command: Sequence[str]) -> bool:
    """
    Decide whether a command is safe enough to run.

    Args:
        command: Parsed command vector.

    Returns:
        True when the command is allowlisted.
    """
    if not command:
        return False

    first = command[0]
    if first not in ALLOWED_COMMANDS:
        return False

    if first == "git":
        allowed_git_subcommands = {"status", "diff", "log", "grep", "show", "rev-parse"}
        if len(command) < 2 or command[1] not in allowed_git_subcommands:
            return False

    if first in {"python", "python3"} and len(command) >= 3 and command[1] == "-m":
        # Allow `python -m pytest` and similar module invocations.
        return True

    return True

def run_shell(command: str, cwd: str | None = None, timeout_sec: int = 120) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Run a restricted command without shell expansion.

    Args:
        command: Command line string to execute.
        cwd: Optional working directory relative to REPO_ROOT.
        timeout_sec: Hard timeout.

    Returns:
        Completed process details.
    """
    args = shlex.split(command)
    if not is_allowed_command(args):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Command is not allowlisted: {args[0] if args else '<empty>'}"
        )

    workdir = REPO_ROOT if cwd is None else ensure_within_repo(REPO_ROOT / cwd)
    start = time.time()

    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(
            args,
            cwd=str(workdir),
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=timeout_sec,
            check=False,
        )
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:
        return {
            "command": command,
            "cwd": str(workdir.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)),
            "status": "timeout",
            "timeout_sec": timeout_sec,
            "stdout": exc.stdout or "",
            "stderr": exc.stderr or "",
            "duration_sec": round(time.time() - start, 3),
        }

    return {
        "command": command,
        "cwd": str(workdir.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)),
        "status": "ok" if proc.returncode == 0 else "error",
        "returncode": proc.returncode,
        "stdout": proc.stdout,
        "stderr": proc.stderr,
        "duration_sec": round(time.time() - start, 3),
    }

def block_to_dict(block: Any) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Convert an Anthropic content block into a plain dictionary.

    Args:
        block: SDK content block object.

    Returns:
        Dictionary form suitable for message replay.
    """
    if isinstance(block, dict):
        return block
    if hasattr(block, "model_dump"):
        return block.model_dump(exclude_none=True)  # type: ignore[no-any-return]
    if hasattr(block, "__dict__"):
        return {k: v for k, v in vars(block).items() if not k.startswith("_")}
    return {"type": "text", "text": str(block)}

def extract_text(blocks: Iterable[Any]) -> str:
    """
    Collect all text blocks from an Anthropic response.

    Args:
        blocks: Response content blocks.

    Returns:
        Concatenated assistant text.
    """
    parts: List[str] = []
    for block in blocks:
        data = block_to_dict(block)
        if data.get("type") == "text":
            text = data.get("text")
            if isinstance(text, str) and text.strip():
                parts.append(text)
    return "\n".join(parts).strip()

def execute_tool(name: str, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    Dispatch a Claude tool call to the matching local implementation.

    Args:
        name: Tool name emitted by Claude.
        payload: Tool input payload.

    Returns:
        JSON-serializable tool result.
    """
    if name == "search_repo":
        return search_repo(
            query=str(payload["query"]),
            max_results=int(payload.get("max_results", 10)),
        )
    if name == "read_file":
        return read_file(
            path=str(payload["path"]),
            start_line=int(payload.get("start_line", 1)),
            end_line=payload.get("end_line"),
        )
    if name == "write_file":
        return write_file(
            path=str(payload["path"]),
            content=str(payload["content"]),
        )
    if name == "run_shell":
        return run_shell(
            command=str(payload["command"]),
            cwd=payload.get("cwd"),
            timeout_sec=int(payload.get("timeout_sec", 120)),
        )
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool: {name}")

def run_agent(user_task: str) -> str:
    """
    Run a full Claude tool-using workflow until Claude returns a final answer.

    Args:
        user_task: The high-level task for the agent.

    Returns:
        Final assistant response text.
    """
    api_key = os.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
    if not api_key:
        raise EnvironmentError("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set")

    client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=api_key)
    messages: List[Dict[str, Any]] = [\
        {\
            "role": "user",\
            "content": (\
                "You are a careful code-fixing agent. "\
                "First gather context, then make the smallest safe change, then verify with tests. "\
                "Do not guess when you can inspect. Keep the reasoning terse and operational.\n\n"\
                f"Task: {user_task}"\
            ),\
        }\
    ]

    for turn in range(1, MAX_TURNS + 1):
        emit_event("model_request", turn=turn, model=MODEL_NAME, messages=len(messages))

        try:
            response = client.messages.create(
                model=MODEL_NAME,
                max_tokens=2048,
                temperature=0,
                tools=TOOLS,
                tool_choice={"type": "auto"},
                messages=messages,
            )
        except Exception as exc:
            emit_event("model_error", turn=turn, error=str(exc))
            raise

        assistant_blocks = [block_to_dict(block) for block in response.content]
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_blocks})

        tool_calls = [b for b in assistant_blocks if b.get("type") == "tool_use"]
        if not tool_calls:
            final_text = extract_text(response.content)
            emit_event("model_final", turn=turn, text_chars=len(final_text))
            return final_text or "(Claude returned no text output.)"

        tool_results: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
        for call in tool_calls:
            tool_name = str(call["name"])
            tool_id = str(call["id"])
            tool_input = call.get("input") or {}
            emit_event("tool_call", turn=turn, tool=tool_name, tool_use_id=tool_id)

            started = time.time()
            try:
                result = execute_tool(tool_name, tool_input)
            except Exception as exc:
                result = {"error": str(exc), "tool": tool_name}
            duration = round(time.time() - started, 3)

            emit_event(
                "tool_result",
                turn=turn,
                tool=tool_name,
                tool_use_id=tool_id,
                duration_sec=duration,
            )

            tool_results.append(
                {
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": tool_id,
                    "content": json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2),
                }
            )

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})

    raise RuntimeError(f"Exceeded MAX_TURNS={MAX_TURNS} without reaching a final answer")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    task = (
        sys.argv[1]
        if len(sys.argv) > 1
        else "Investigate the failing authentication tests, fix the root cause, and verify the fix."
    )
    print(run_agent(task))
```

The code is doing exactly what Claude’s docs describe at the protocol level. Claude returns a structured tool request, your client executes the tool in the environment you control, then the tool result goes back into the conversation and Claude continues. That is the same “client SDK tool loop” that Anthropic contrasts with the Agent SDK, where Claude handles the loop for you.

### How to execute the example in practice

For the real scenario, start the agent with a failing test command or a CI log pasted into the prompt. The agent should first search for the error or module names, then read the relevant files, then patch the smallest viable change, then run the same test command again. This is aligned with Anthropic’s documented advice to use specific reproduction commands and stack traces for bug fixing, and to verify refactors or changes with tests before considering the task complete.

For safety and operability, keep the agent in `plan` mode when exploring an unfamiliar codebase, use `acceptEdits` only when you are comfortable with automated file changes, and reserve more permissive modes for isolated environments. Anthropic’s permission-mode docs make clear that `plan` is read-only, `acceptEdits` allows file edits and common filesystem commands, and `auto` is intended for long tasks with background safety checks. They also note that writes to protected paths are not auto-approved outside bypass mode, which is a useful guardrail for repository integrity.

### The architectural trade-off

The strongest pattern is to keep the model responsible for reasoning and tool selection, while keeping your application responsible for execution control, path safety, audit logs, command allowlists, and timeouts. That separation gives you the flexibility of an agent without surrendering operational safety. If the workflow gets large, Anthropic’s own subagent design is the cleanest way to reduce context bloat: explore in one context, plan in another, and keep the main session focused on the actual change.

## Agent Teams vs Subagents

Anthropic recently introduced Agent Teams.

Subagents:

```
Parent Agent
    │
    ├── Worker
    ├── Worker
    └── Worker
```

Workers report only to parent.

Agent Teams:

```
Lead Agent
      │
      ▼Shared Task Board      │
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼Agent A
Agent B
Agent C
```

Agents communicate directly and coordinate through a shared task list. Anthropic recommends Agent Teams for large multi-component engineering initiatives where workers need ongoing coordination rather than simple delegated research.

### Pipe Claude Into Scripts

This is the workflow that transforms Claude into infrastructure.

Instead of interactive usage:

```

you execute:

```

```

Headless mode.

Now Claude becomes part of automation pipelines.

Example:

```

```

Workflow:

    │

### Complete Enterprise Architecture

When all Claude workflow primitives are combined, the architecture becomes:

```
                       Lead Claude
                         │
                         ▼               Planning Session                         │
        ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
        ▼                ▼                ▼   Research        Implementation     Validation
   Subagent         Subagent          Subagent        ▼                ▼                ▼     Worktree A      Worktree B      Worktree C        ▼                ▼                ▼     Findings          Changes          Tests        └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                         ▼                    Final PR                         ▼                    CI Pipeline                         ▼                  Claude Review
```

This is no longer prompt engineering.

This is an agent orchestration platform.

The deeper insight from Claude Code’s workflow design is that Anthropic is moving toward a software engineering operating model where the LLM is not merely generating code. It is acting as a planner, coordinator, researcher, implementer, reviewer, and validator, while Git worktrees provide isolation, subagents provide parallel cognition, sessions provide long-term continuity, and CI integration provides operational automation. That combination is what makes Claude Code one of the first genuinely production-oriented agentic development systems rather than just a coding chatbot.
